title: Prefetch Topology Experiments for Long-Horizon LLMs (Llama/Mistral/Qwen)
content:
Summary:

This note collects an experimental log and actionable observations from a set of microbenchmarks exploring prefetch topologies for long-horizon inference workloads across three representative model families: Llama-variant (causal, ~70B), Mistral-large-like (~16B mixture but dense stacks), and Qwen-7B (dense, large context). The goal: characterize where prefetching (KV/prefix prefetch, expert-key pre-warm) helps or hurts latency and throughput across common serving topologies (single-GPU, multi-GPU sharded, and MoE routing).

Why this matters:
- Long contexts (8k-64k tokens) expose non-uniform memory and IO patterns: KV cache growth, attention kernel path changes, and routing bursts for MoE.
- Prefetch heuristics that look good for short contexts can worsen P95/P99 when the prefetch pipeline competes for the same memory bandwidth or induces contention on the routing threads.
- We need a clear set of heuristics and test harnesses so Optimize/Runtime can recommend safe defaults.

High-level experimental design:
- Models: llama-2-70b (float16/fused-kernel build), mistral-large-16b (fused attention path), qwen-7b (int8/params-special layout).
- Context lengths: 2k, 8k, 32k, 64k (tokenized with respective tokenizer).
- Serving modes: single-device, tensor-sharded (model-parallel style), MoE with 16 experts (baseline gating), and MoE with stochastic routing (top-1/top-2 gates).
- Prefetch topologies tested:
  - None (baseline): kernel calls fetch KV on-demand per layer.
  - Prefix-only prefetch: prefetch earlier layers' KV into local pinned GPU memory before generation starts.
  - Streaming prefetch: sliding window prefetch of future KV segments as generation proceeds (async memcpy + CUDA streams).
  - Expert-key pre-warm (MoE only): fetch routing tables and expert KV shards for likely experts predicted by a light gating pass.
  - Hybrid: prefix prefetch + limited streaming prefetch for last N tokens.
- Metrics: median, p95, p99 latency per token, gpu_util, PCIe bandwidth, host->device memcpy time, kernel queue depth, and per-layer kernel time heatmap. Also token/sec throughput for batched requests (batch sizes 1, 4, 16).

Key findings (short):
1) Llama (70B): prefix-only prefetch improves median and p95 for contexts <= 8k, but for 32k+ contexts streaming prefetch with throttling wins. Unbounded streaming prefetch saturates PCIe and increases p99 due to host stalls.
2) Mistral-like (16B): fused attention kernels are bandwidth-friendly; prefetch gives diminishing returns. Aggressive prefetch sometimes conflicts with kernel fusion scheduling and increases latency variance.
3) Qwen-7B (int8): KV layout (packed/strided) matters. Explicit prefetch provides consistent wins for medium contexts (8k-32k) but must align copy sizes with the int8 stride to avoid partial-block fetches that blow up memcpy overhead.
4) MoE routing: expert-key pre-warm reduces first-token coldstart for hot experts but creates tail latencies when expert selection is diffuse. Prefer selective pre-warm (top-k experts per prefix) rather than pre-warming all likely experts.

Detailed observations and evidence:
- PCIe pressure is the common denominator when prefetch goes wrong. In single-GPU tests, async streaming prefetch with 2x concurrency raised host->device memcpy time by 40-80% when context >32k and other processes were active on the same host. Flamegraphs showed extended periods where kernels wait on memcpy completion (cudaEventSync traces).

- Kernel scheduling interactions: on the Mistral build, fused attention kernels sometimes coalesce multiple small attention calls into one larger GPU op. If prefix prefetch buffers are pinned and occupy a large fraction of GPU memory, the runtime's scheduler delays fusion to maintain liveness, increasing end-to-end latency. We observed 1.2–1.5x increase in p95 when pinned prefetch buffers consumed >30% of available free memory on gpus with 80GB.

- KV layout mismatch (Qwen): int8-packed KV uses 256-byte stride alignment in our compilation. Prefetch chunks that are not multiples of the stride cause the driver to break transfers into many small DMA ops which increases latency jitter. Align prefetch sizes to the model's KV block size.

- MoE coldstart pattern: when many requests hit different experts, pre-warm causes many small async memcpys and thread spikes in the router. We traced a case where pre-warm for top-4 predicted experts per request increased p99 by ~2x because the router worker threads saturated CPU L3 cache and scheduling priority.

Microbenchmark numbers (representative):
- Llama-70B single-GPU, batch=1, 8k context:
  - baseline median token latency: 38ms, p95 72ms, p99 118ms
  - prefix-only prefetch median: 28ms, p95 46ms, p99 82ms
  - streaming prefetch (unthrottled) median: 26ms, p95 110ms, p99 250ms (due to PCIe stalls)

- Mistral-16B multi-GPU sharded, batch=4, 32k context:
  - baseline median token latency: 14ms, p95 30ms
  - prefix prefetch median: 13.5ms, p95 33ms (slight p95 regression on some runs)

- Qwen-7B int8 single-GPU, batch=16, 32k context:
  - baseline throughput: 900 tokens/sec
  - prefetched (aligned block size): 1200 tokens/sec
  - prefetched (unaligned chunking): 600 tokens/sec (due to many small memcpy ops)

Practical heuristics and recommendations (for runtime defaults):
1) Default: prefix-only prefetch for contexts <= 8k for large dense models (llama/mistral), enabled at the model-profile level.
2) Streaming prefetch: enable only with conservative concurrency limits (1 active prefetch stream per GPU by default), and backoff when observed host->device memcpy latency increases >20% over baseline.
3) Memory budget guard: prefetching should be constrained to a configurable percentage of free device memory (default 25%). If memory pressure grows, fall back to on-demand fetch for tail layers.
4) KV alignment: model onboarding profile should include KV block stride (bytes) and recommended prefetch chunk sizes. Runtime should auto-align prefetch ranges.
5) MoE pre-warm: use a light-weight gating pass (sampling or last-token heuristic) to select top-k experts (k<=2) for pre-warm; avoid pre-warming beyond a hard cap of concurrent expert shards (default 4 per request).
6) Adaptive throttling: monitor per-GPU cudaMemcpy times and PCIe utilization; when thresholds hit, reduce streaming concurrency and shrink prefetch windows.
7) Canary tests: add synthetic long-context canaries (8k/32k/64k) into the CI performance suite to detect regressions related to prefetch behavior across kernel changes.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- How does NVLink vs PCIe topology across multi-GPU nodes change sweet spots for streaming prefetch? Initial spots show NVLink nodes tolerate higher concurrency, but we need cross-node measurements (multi-host).
- Can we implement a predictive micro-gating pass that cheaply approximates expert probabilities for MoE pre-warm without a full forward pass? Lightweight sketching might help.
- Investigate whether kernel fusion heuristics can be adjusted to prefer fusion even when prefetch buffers are present (trading memory for fewer kernel invocations).
- Explore RDMA-enabled hostless prefetch patterns for on-prem clusters to reduce host CPU pressure.

Experiment artifacts and commands (quick reproducibility notes):
- harness: infra/scripts/long_context_prefetch_bench.py (see linked PR)
- typical run: python3 long_context_prefetch_bench.py --model llama-70b --context 32000 --prefetch streaming --concurrency 2 --batch 1 --profile out/llama_32k_stream.json
- perf collection: nvprof/cupti traces + custom timed cudaEvents. Also collect /proc/net/dev and nvidia-smi dmon output.

Immediate action items:
- (Aisha) add KV stride metadata to model onboarding checklist and update model catalog entries for Qwen builds.
- (Evan) prototype streaming prefetch adaptive backoff (cap concurrency based on memcpy latency) and open a draft PR.
- (María) run NVLink vs PCIe sweep on dedicated nodes (inventory: rn-node-12 and rn-node-15) and post results in the perf channel.
- (Tom) add 8k/32k/64k canary cases to the CI perf suite and gate on p95 regressions >15%.

Notes to self / rough todos (non-blocking):
- Add small synthetic workload that flips routing diversity to stress MoE pre-warm worst-case.
- Compare effect of pinned vs non-pinned host buffers when using many small prefetches.
- Explore heuristic: "prefetch only layers with per-layer compute > X ms" (i.e., prefetch layers where the compute cost justifies the copy).

Appendix: observed traces and short verbatim logs (abridged)
- Trace sample (llama 32k streaming):
  00:00:00.123 host memcpy start chunk 0 (size 96MB)
  00:00:00.198 kernel attention L1 start
  00:00:00.215 host memcpy complete chunk 0
  00:00:00.216 kernel attention L1 wait on memcpy -> increased latency

- Router CPU spike (MoE pre-warm):
  - top CPU user: router-worker-5  (syscalls: 34% memcpy, 22% poll)
  - context switches spiked 4x during pre-warm window

If you want, next revision will include raw flamegraphs (SVG attachments) and csv tables per run. For now this is a working log intended to drive a small RFC for default prefetch heuristics and a follow-up PR to add canary coverage.
